blocks.content: The CIDR topic showed you how to read and write a range of IP addresses using slash notation. Subnetting is the practical, deliberate act of taking one larger address block and dividing it into several smaller ones, each one becoming its own separate, organized subnet.

If CIDR is the notation, subnetting is what you actually do with it, splitting one big network into purposeful, manageable pieces, exactly the kind of thing a growing office or a cloud environment needs to do constantly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015293330-686061666.png
blocks.alt: One large network block deliberately divided into several smaller, purpose specific subnets

blocks.content: 1. Why Divide a Network at All
blocks.text: 1. Why Divide a Network at All

blocks.content: One giant, flat, undivided network has real practical problems as it grows. Broadcast traffic, messages meant for every device on the network, spreads to literally everyone, even devices that have nothing to do with it, and there is no real separation between different groups of devices, engineering machines, sales machines, and guest devices all mixed together with no isolation at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015295246-285628346.png
blocks.alt: A flat network floods broadcast traffic everywhere; subnetting contains it and provides real isolation between groups

blocks.content: Subnetting fixes this by deliberately splitting one large network into smaller, purposeful subnets, each with contained broadcast traffic and real separation from the others.
2. The Core Mechanism: Borrowing Host Bits
blocks.text: 2. The Core Mechanism: Borrowing Host Bits

blocks.content: Recall from the CIDR topic that a network prefix length determines how many bits are fixed, the network part, versus free to vary, the host part. Subnetting works by borrowing some of those free host bits and turning them into additional fixed bits, creating several smaller networks out of one larger one.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015296746-638955506.png
blocks.alt: Subnetting borrows bits from the host portion, turning one larger network into several smaller ones

blocks.content: 3. A Full Worked Example

Start with 192.168.1.0/24, a single block of 256 addresses. Borrowing 2 host bits moves the prefix from /24 to /26, and since 2 borrowed bits give 4 possible combinations, this single /24 splits cleanly into four separate /26 subnets, each with 64 addresses.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015298330-166922659.png
blocks.alt: Borrowing 2 bits splits one /24 block of 256 addresses into four /26 subnets of 64 addresses each

blocks.content: 4. Not Every Address in a Subnet Is Usable
blocks.text: 4. Not Every Address in a Subnet Is Usable

blocks.content: Within each individual subnet, two specific addresses are reserved and cannot be assigned to any actual device. The very first address in the subnet is the network address, identifying the subnet itself. The very last address in the subnet is the broadcast address, used to reach every device on that subnet at once.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015299834-389040222.png
blocks.alt: The first address in a subnet identifies it; the last address is reserved for reaching every device on it at once

blocks.title: A real, practical consequence
blocks.content: A /26 subnet has 64 total addresses, but only 62 of them are actually usable for devices, since the first and last are reserved. This same pattern applies to every subnet size, always subtract exactly two for the usable count.
5. Subnet Masks: An Older, Equivalent Notation
blocks.text: 5. Subnet Masks: An Older, Equivalent Notation

blocks.content: Before CIDR slash notation became standard, the same information was written as a subnet mask, a full 32 bit pattern spelled out in dotted decimal form. A /26 prefix is exactly equivalent to the subnet mask 255.255.255.192, both describe the identical split between fixed and free bits, just in different notations you may still encounter in older documentation or configuration screens.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015301401-722486966.png
blocks.alt: A CIDR prefix like /26 and its equivalent subnet mask like 255.255.255.192 describe exactly the same thing

blocks.content: 6. The Real Benefit: Isolation

Once split into separate subnets, each one genuinely gets its own contained broadcast domain. Traffic meant for every device on the Engineering subnet stays within Engineering, it does not spill over and flood the Sales subnet or vice versa. This containment is a real, practical benefit, not just an organizational nicety.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015302915-100922556.png
blocks.alt: Each subnet gets its own contained broadcast domain, keeping traffic isolated from other subnets

blocks.content: 7. A Real World Example

A growing company office network is a natural, relatable example. Different floors, or different departments, each get their own subnet, and a guest WiFi network gets its own separate subnet entirely, deliberately isolated from internal company systems, so a guest device on that network has no direct path to reach sensitive internal machines at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015304451-585589553.png
blocks.alt: A real office network commonly splits into per floor subnets plus a separate, isolated guest WiFi subnet

blocks.title: The guest WiFi pattern is genuinely common
blocks.content: Almost every real office and even many home routers now offer a separate guest network specifically for this reason, a visitor device gets internet access without ever being able to reach printers, file servers, or anything else on the main internal subnet.
8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming every address in a subnet range is usable for a device, when the first and last are always reserved for the network and broadcast addresses.","Confusing CIDR notation and subnet masks as different concepts, when they are just two different ways of writing the exact same information.","Subnetting divides one larger network into several smaller, purposeful ones by borrowing host bits.","Each subnet has its own network address, broadcast address, and a smaller set of actually usable addresses.","Subnetting provides real broadcast traffic containment and isolation between groups of devices."]
items: Assuming every address in a subnet range is usable for a device, when the first and last are always reserved for the network and broadcast addresses.
Confusing CIDR notation and subnet masks as different concepts, when they are just two different ways of writing the exact same information.
Subnetting divides one larger network into several smaller, purposeful ones by borrowing host bits.
Each subnet has its own network address, broadcast address, and a smaller set of actually usable addresses.
Subnetting provides real broadcast traffic containment and isolation between groups of devices.
